title: Operate Fleets with Ad-Hoc Modules
objective: Choose safe modules and target groups for one-off fleet operations.

paragraphs: Ad-hoc commands are ideal for discovery, diagnosis, and isolated changes that do not yet deserve a playbook. A host pattern selects inventory members and a module performs one focused operation in parallel.

Facts reveal the remote environment. Purpose-built modules manage packages, users, files, services, cron entries, source checkouts, and asynchronous jobs more safely than shell commands because they understand state.
Target narrowly, use check mode when supported, and convert recurring commands into version-controlled playbooks. OpenSSH connection reuse and pipelining can reduce overhead on large fleets.
explanation.rule: Use a module for state changes; reserve shell or command for work with no suitable module.

examples.note: This planning map records intent before any host is contacted.

checks.question: When should an ad-hoc command become a playbook?
options: When the operation must be repeated or reviewed
Whenever only one host is targeted

feedback.incorrect: Repeatable operations belong in version control as playbooks.

checks.question: The ansible.builtin.ping module reports UNREACHABLE for web01. What should you investigate first?
options: SSH connectivity and inventory connection variables
The remote ICMP firewall rule only

feedback.correct: Correct—the module logs in over Ansible’s connection transport and executes Python; it is not an ICMP echo.
feedback.incorrect: Ansible ping is a connection-and-module test. Check inventory, credentials, SSH, and remote Python.

lab.title: Mission: inspect the disposable fleet
lab.setup: Start the lab with npm run lab:up, open the Terminal tab, and work from /workspace.
steps: Run ansible all -m ansible.builtin.ping and predict how many hosts should return pong.
Repeat with --limit web01 and explain why only one host appears.
lab.success: The inventory lists web01, web02, and db01; both webservers return SUCCESS.
